title: Story of a Soul (1898)
hookLine: Thérèse's memoir is published and goes around the world

cards: A notebook, a pen, and a young nun in a Carmelite convent in Lisieux, in France. Her older sister, who is also her prioress, has asked her to write down memories of their childhood.
So Thérèse writes: her family, her mother's death, her tears, her first communion, the convent. Later, already sick, she is asked to write more, and she keeps going in a garden chair, then in bed.
She began it for her sisters, not for strangers; only near the end does she speak of the pages being printed. After she dies, the convent prints them: Story of a Soul.

teach.b: Follow the book. First, the writing. Thérèse wrote in pieces, under obedience, in ordinary notebooks.
She wasn't composing a classic; she was answering her sisters.

Second, the editing. Her sister Pauline, Mother Agnes, prepared the pages for print and smoothed them in places. Much later, the original notebooks were published as Thérèse wrote them, so readers could see her own words.
Third, the spreading. Carmelite convents would send a short account of a sister's life to other houses after her death. This one was different.
It was copied, reprinted, translated, passed from hand to hand. Tradition says letters came back to Lisieux from readers: soldiers, mothers, missionaries, people in prison.
Fourth, the little way. What readers found was not a story of great deeds but a way: do small things with love, trust God like a child, and don't wait to become impressive first.
In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Thérèse took that line seriously.
The Church later canonized her and named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. Much of what she taught reached readers through one little book, written for her sisters.

how: Some Catholics read Story of a Soul on retreat or around Thérèse's feast in October, and parishes and prayer groups sometimes read it together a chapter at a time.

games.why: she kept writing, in pencil, in a garden chair and then in bed, until she couldn't.

practice: If you have the book, open it anywhere and read one page slowly; if not, take today's line, become as little children.

Then go through one small task from today in your mind, a dish, a message, a chore you've been avoiding, slowly, done with care. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, notice how small and how real it is.

wordCard.voice: Little way. Thérèse's idea that small things done with love, and trusting God like a child, matter more than impressive deeds: the heart of Story of a Soul.
